title: Normalization & Data Modeling
tagline: Design schemas where every fact lives in one place, from ER diagrams and functional dependencies through BCNF to migrations and document modeling.

sections.content:
A schema outlives the code that first used it. Services get rewritten, frameworks change, teams turn over, but the tables and the data in them stay, often for a decade or more. A good data model makes correct code easy to write: every fact lives in one place, the database rejects impossible states, and new features slot in without rewrites. A poor one forces every engineer, forever, to remember to update the same fact in three places, and someone eventually forgets.

**Data modeling** is the discipline of turning a messy description of a business ("students enroll in courses, each taught by an instructor...") into entities, relationships and constraints. **Normalization** is the formal toolkit for checking that model: you write down the **functional dependencies** (which facts determine which other facts) and decompose tables until every dependency is enforced by a key. The normal forms (1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF) are not bureaucracy. Each one removes a specific class of **anomaly**, where an ordinary INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE corrupts or loses information.

This chapter follows **one running example**, a university enrollment spreadsheet, from an unnormalized sheet all the way to BCNF, then covers the practical side of modeling:
- ER modeling, cardinality and many-to-many junction tables,
- keys: candidate, primary, foreign, and surrogate vs natural,
- when and how to **denormalize** deliberately (read-heavy paths, analytics, caches, star schemas),
- soft deletes, JSONB columns vs tables, and zero-downtime **expand/contract migrations**,
- how document databases change the trade-off with **embed vs reference**.

The ACID & Indexes chapter has a one-page summary of the normal forms. This chapter is the full treatment, with every step worked through on the same data.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["Requirements and access patterns"] --> B["Conceptual model: entities, relationships, cardinality"]
  B --> C["Logical schema: tables, keys, foreign keys"]
  C --> D["List functional dependencies"]
  D --> E{"Every determinant a key?"}
  E -->|"No"| F["Decompose: 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF"]
  F --> D
  E -->|"Yes"| G["Physical design: types, indexes, constraints"]
  G --> H["Measure real queries"]
  H --> I["Denormalize deliberately where reads demand it"]
sections.caption: The modeling loop. Normalize first so the model is correct, then denormalize specific paths with evidence. Never skip straight to a denormalized design.

sections.title: One Fact, One Place
sections.content:
Picture a company where every team keeps its own spreadsheet of customer addresses. Sales has one, billing has one, shipping has one. A customer moves house and tells sales. Sales updates its sheet. Billing keeps sending invoices to the old address, and shipping sends a parcel there too. No single edit was wrong. The *design* guaranteed the inconsistency, because one fact (where the customer lives) was stored in three places.

The fix is not "remind everyone to update all three sheets". The fix is a single address book that everyone *references* by customer ID. Then an address change is one edit, and every team sees it immediately.

Normalization is that principle applied with rigour: **every fact is stored exactly once, next to the thing it describes, and everything else points to it.** The normal forms give you a checklist for finding facts that are stored in the wrong place: a course title repeated on every enrollment row, or a department name copied onto every course.

Denormalization is choosing, with your eyes open, to keep a *copy* of the address in the shipping sheet because shipping prints 10,000 labels an hour and cannot wait for a lookup. That can be the right call, but now someone owns keeping the copy in sync.

sections.title: ER Modeling: Entities, Relationships and Cardinality
sections.content:
**Entity-Relationship (ER) modeling** (Peter Chen, 1976) describes a domain before any table exists:
- An **entity** is a thing with independent identity that you store facts about: Student, Course, Department, Instructor.
- An **attribute** is a fact about an entity: `student_name`, `course_title`.
- A **relationship** is an association between entities: a student *enrolls in* a course, and a department *offers* courses. A relationship can carry its own attributes. `grade` belongs to neither the student nor the course, only to the enrollment.

**Cardinality** says how many instances can participate on each side. **Optionality** (participation) says whether participation is required:
- **One-to-one (1:1)**: user ↔ user_settings. Implement with a foreign key that is also UNIQUE (often the child's PK is the parent's PK). Ask why it isn't one table. Valid reasons are optional or sparse data, different access or security rules, or a very wide row.
- **One-to-many (1:N)**: department → courses. Put a foreign key on the **many** side (`course.dept_code`). `NOT NULL` on the FK means "every course must belong to a department" (mandatory participation).
- **Many-to-many (M:N)**: students ↔ courses. A relational table cannot hold a list in a cell, so you add a **junction table** (also called an associative, bridge or join table): `enrollment(student_id, course_code, ...)` with a foreign key to each side and a composite primary key (or a surrogate key plus a UNIQUE constraint on the pair). The junction table is often a real entity in its own right with its own attributes (grade, enrolled_at, status). Name it after the business concept (`enrollment`, `membership`, `order_line`), not `student_course`.

In **crow's-foot notation**, which most ER tools use, a line ending in a three-pronged "crow's foot" means *many*, a bar means *one*, and a circle means *optional (zero)*. Mermaid's `erDiagram` renders this, but this app draws schemas with class diagrams, using `"1" -- "0..*"` multiplicities, which carry the same information.

Modeling questions to ask the domain expert, because the answers become constraints:
- Can a course exist with no instructor? (optional vs mandatory)
- Can an instructor teach more than one course? (1:N vs M:N)
- Can a student take the same course twice, for example after failing it? (this changes the junction table's key)
- When an instructor leaves, what happens to past enrollments? (ON DELETE behaviour, history)

sections.caption: The final enrollment model. Enrollment is the junction table that resolves the student and course many-to-many relationship and carries the grade. Each instructor teaches exactly one course, and a course can have several instructors (sections).

sections.title: Keys: Candidate, Primary, Foreign, Surrogate vs Natural
sections.content:
A **superkey** is any set of columns whose values uniquely identify a row. A **candidate key** is a *minimal* superkey: remove any column and it stops being unique. A table can have several. In `student`, both `student_id` and `email` are candidate keys.
- The **primary key** is the candidate key you choose as the main identifier. It is `NOT NULL`, unique, and what foreign keys reference.
- The other candidate keys are **alternate keys**. Enforce them with `UNIQUE NOT NULL`. A candidate key that is not declared unique is a bug waiting for a duplicate.
- A **composite key** has several columns, like `(student_id, course_code)` in a junction table.
- A **foreign key** is a column (or set of columns) whose values must exist as a key in the referenced table. It is the database-enforced form of a relationship. Choose the `ON DELETE` action deliberately: `RESTRICT`/`NO ACTION` (the default, which blocks the delete), `CASCADE` (delete the children, right for owned data like phone numbers), or `SET NULL`. Index foreign key columns on the child side. PostgreSQL does not do it automatically, and without the index every parent delete scans the child table.

**Natural vs surrogate keys.** A **natural key** comes from the domain: `dept_code = 'CS'`, ISO country codes, an ISBN. A **surrogate key** is a meaningless generated identifier: an identity integer or a UUID.
- Natural keys are readable and save a join, but the real world changes them. People change emails and names, "unique" government IDs have duplicates and privacy rules, and companies rebrand product codes. Changing a primary key means updating every foreign key that points at it.
- Surrogate keys never need to change, and they are compact (8 bytes for `bigint`). The common practice: **use a surrogate primary key, and still put a UNIQUE constraint on the natural key**. Without that, the database will happily store the same student twice under two ids.
- Short, stable, standardized codes (`dept_code`, currency `USD`) make perfectly good natural primary keys.

**Choosing a surrogate type in 2026:**
- `bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` (SQL standard, preferred over the legacy `serial`) is compact and fast. Exposing it in URLs leaks volume ("order 10,523") and invites enumeration, so pair it with authorization checks or a separate public id.
- **UUIDv4** is random, so it can be generated anywhere without coordination, but random inserts scatter across the B-tree and hurt cache locality on large tables.
- **UUIDv7** (RFC 9562, 2024) starts with a millisecond timestamp, so values are roughly time-ordered and index-friendly. PostgreSQL 18 includes a built-in `uuidv7()` function. On older versions, generate it in the application or with an extension. It is a good default when ids must be generated client-side or across services. Note that it reveals the creation time.

sections.title: Functional Dependencies: The Rules Behind the Normal Forms
sections.content:
A **functional dependency (FD)** `X → Y` means: any two rows that agree on X must agree on Y. In words, X *determines* Y. FDs come from **business rules**, not from looking at sample data. Three rows that happen to share a value prove nothing, but "each course has exactly one title" is a rule.

For the enrollment domain, the rules give these FDs:
1. `student_id → student_name`
2. `course_code → course_title, dept_code`
3. `dept_code → dept_name`
4. `student_id, course_code → instructor, grade` (a student takes a course once, in one section)
5. `instructor → course_code` (each instructor teaches exactly one course, and a course can have several instructors)

**Armstrong's axioms** let you derive new FDs from these:
- **reflexivity**: if Y ⊆ X then X → Y,
- **augmentation**: if X → Y then XZ → YZ,
- **transitivity**: if X → Y and Y → Z then X → Z.

For example, 2 and 3 together give `course_code → dept_name` by transitivity.

The **attribute closure** X⁺ is the set of everything X determines. You compute it by repeatedly applying FDs until nothing new is added. **X is a superkey exactly when X⁺ contains every attribute.** Here `{student_id, course_code}⁺` is all 8 attributes, so it is a key. Less obviously, `{student_id, instructor}⁺` is also everything: instructor gives course_code, and then FD 4 applies. So the table has **two candidate keys**, a detail that matters for BCNF later.

Vocabulary used by the normal forms:
- A **prime attribute** is part of *some* candidate key (here: student_id, course_code, instructor).
- A **partial dependency** is a non-prime attribute that depends on *part* of a composite key (`student_id → student_name`).
- A **transitive dependency** is a non-prime attribute that depends on another non-prime attribute (`course_code → dept_code → dept_name`).
- A **determinant** is the left side of an FD.

sections.title: The Running Example and Its Anomalies
sections.content:
The registrar's original spreadsheet, **unnormalized (UNF)**: one row per student, with a list of phones and a repeating group of enrollments packed into cells.

| student_id | student_name | phones | enrollments |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Ana | 555-0101, 555-0102 | CS101 (Intro to Programming, CS, Computer Science, Dr. Lee, A); MA201 (Linear Algebra, MA, Mathematics, Dr. Kim, B) |
| 2 | Ben | 555-0200 | CS101 (Intro to Programming, CS, Computer Science, Dr. Park, B+) |

Even flattened into one row per enrollment (shown in the next section), the sheet suffers three classic **anomalies**:
- **Update anomaly.** The department "Computer Science" is renamed "Computing". Its name is stored on *every* CS enrollment row, so the rename must touch all of them. Miss one (a failed batch, a concurrent insert using the old name) and the database now holds two different names for department CS. The data contradicts itself.
- **Insertion anomaly.** The university creates course CS301 and hires Dr. Ito to teach it, but no student has enrolled yet. There is nowhere to record that CS301 is called "Algorithms" or that Dr. Ito teaches it, because every row needs a student_id as part of its key.
- **Deletion anomaly.** Ana drops MA201. Deleting her enrollment row also deletes the only record that MA201 is "Linear Algebra", that it belongs to Mathematics, and that Dr. Kim teaches it. You lose facts about other things.

Each anomaly is a symptom of the same disease: **a fact stored in a row whose key does not determine it.** The department name depends on dept_code, but it is stored in a table keyed by (student_id, course_code). The normal forms find these misplaced facts systematically.

sections.title: First and Second Normal Form
sections.content:
**First Normal Form (1NF): atomic values, no repeating groups, a key.** Every cell holds one value of the column's type, there are no "phone1, phone2, phone3" column groups, and every row is uniquely identifiable. Split the phone list into its own table, and give each enrollment its own row:

**enrollment (1NF)**, key (student_id, course_code)
| student_id | course_code | student_name | course_title | dept_code | dept_name | instructor | grade |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | CS101 | Ana | Intro to Programming | CS | Computer Science | Dr. Lee | A |
| 1 | MA201 | Ana | Linear Algebra | MA | Mathematics | Dr. Kim | B |
| 2 | CS101 | Ben | Intro to Programming | CS | Computer Science | Dr. Park | B+ |

**student_phone (1NF)**, key (student_id, phone): (1, 555-0101), (1, 555-0102), (2, 555-0200)

Now "which students have phone 555-0200?" is an indexed equality lookup instead of a substring search, and adding a third phone needs no schema change. "Atomic" is about how you *query* the value. A `date` or a full `email` is atomic even though it has parts. A comma-separated list you search inside is not. PostgreSQL arrays and JSONB blur the line; see the JSONB section for when that is acceptable.

**Second Normal Form (2NF): no partial dependencies.** Every non-prime attribute must depend on the *whole* of every candidate key, not just part of it. The 1NF table violates this:
- `student_name` depends only on `student_id`,
- `course_title`, `dept_code` and `dept_name` depend only on `course_code`.

Move each partial dependency into a table keyed by the part it depends on (key columns in bold):
- student(**student_id**, student_name)
- course(**course_code**, course_title, dept_code, dept_name)
- enrollment(**student_id, course_code**, instructor, grade)

The student name is now stored once, and a course can exist with no enrollments, which fixes the insertion anomaly for courses. A table whose key is a single column is automatically in 2NF, because there is no "part" of the key to depend on.

sections.title: Third Normal Form and Boyce-Codd Normal Form
sections.content:
**Third Normal Form (3NF): no transitive dependencies.** Formally, for every non-trivial FD X → A, either X is a superkey or A is a prime attribute. Informally: *every non-key column states a fact about the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.*

`course(course_code, course_title, dept_code, dept_name)` violates 3NF: `dept_name` depends on `dept_code`, which is not a key of `course`. This is exactly the update anomaly from the rename. Split it:
- department(**dept_code**, dept_name)
- course(**course_code**, course_title, dept_code → department)

Renaming a department is now a one-row UPDATE. The other tables (student, enrollment) are already in 3NF. In enrollment, `instructor → course_code` has a non-superkey on the left, but course_code is *prime* (part of the key), so 3NF allows it.

**Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF): every determinant is a superkey.** BCNF drops 3NF's "or A is prime" escape hatch. It only differs from 3NF when a table has **overlapping composite candidate keys**, which is exactly our enrollment table: the keys are {student_id, course_code} and {student_id, instructor}, and `instructor → course_code` has a determinant that is not a superkey. The remaining anomaly: "Dr. Park teaches CS101" is stored on every one of Dr. Park's enrollment rows. You cannot record a new instructor's course until a student enrolls, and an update could leave Dr. Park teaching two courses.

The BCNF decomposition:
- teaching(**instructor**, course_code)
- enrollment(**student_id, instructor**, grade)

This decomposition is **lossless**: the shared column `instructor` is a key of `teaching`, so joining the two tables gives back exactly the original rows and no spurious ones. (In general, splitting R into R1 and R2 is lossless when R1 ∩ R2 is a key of R1 or of R2.)

But it is **not dependency-preserving**. The rule "a student takes each course at most once", `{student_id, course_code} → instructor`, now spans two tables, and no single table's key can enforce it. Ana could enroll with both Dr. Lee and Dr. Park for CS101. This is the textbook trade-off:
- **3NF can always be reached losslessly while preserving every dependency.**
- **BCNF is always lossless, but sometimes loses dependencies.**

The practical resolution, used in the schema below, is to give instructor its own table (the BCNF fact), keep `course_code` on enrollment with `PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_code)`, and add a **composite foreign key** `(instructor_id, course_code) → instructor` so the copy can never disagree. Every rule is then enforced by a constraint.

**Beyond BCNF**: 4NF removes multi-valued dependencies (independent lists, such as a person's skills and languages, stored in one table and forced into a cross product). 5NF deals with join dependencies. You will rarely need these by name, but "two independent lists in one table" is a real smell.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  U["UNF: one row per student, phone list and enrollment groups in cells"]
  U -->|"atomic values, one row per fact"| N1["1NF: enrollment with 8 columns, key student_id + course_code, plus student_phone"]
  N1 -->|"remove partial dependencies"| S["student: student_id, student_name"]
  N1 -->|"remove partial dependencies"| C2["course: course_code, title, dept_code, dept_name"]
  N1 -->|"remove partial dependencies"| E2["enrollment: student_id, course_code, instructor, grade"]
  C2 -->|"3NF: remove transitive dependency"| D["department: dept_code, dept_name"]
  C2 -->|"3NF"| C3["course: course_code, title, dept_code"]
  E2 -->|"BCNF: instructor is a determinant"| T["teaching: instructor, course_code"]
  E2 -->|"BCNF"| E4["enrollment: student_id, instructor, grade"]
sections.caption: The running example decomposed step by step. Each arrow moves one misplaced functional dependency into a table where its determinant is the key.

sections.label: FD checker
sections.explanation: This is the textbook algorithm in about 40 lines. `closure` repeatedly applies FDs until nothing new is added, and an attribute set is a superkey when its closure covers the relation. It confirms that the 1NF table has two candidate keys, lists every misplaced dependency, and shows that the 3NF enrollment table is the only one that still violates BCNF, because of `instructor -> course_code`. Run it with `node`. The output matches the comments.

sections.label: Final schema
sections.explanation: Every business rule is now a constraint: phones are rows (1NF), names live with their keys (2NF/3NF), the instructor-to-course fact lives in `instructor` (BCNF), and the composite foreign key plus the `(student_id, course_code)` primary key enforce the dependency that a pure BCNF split would lose. The two rejected INSERTs and their error messages come from actually running the script on PostgreSQL. The final join rebuilds the original spreadsheet view on demand, from data that can no longer contradict itself.

sections.title: When to Denormalize, and the Star Schema
sections.content:
Normalization optimizes for **write correctness**: one fact, one place. Reads pay for it with joins. On an OLTP system with good indexes, joining five tables to fetch one order is usually sub-millisecond, so **normalize by default and denormalize only with evidence**, such as an `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, a latency budget, or a hot path in your profiler.

Legitimate reasons to denormalize:
- **Read-heavy hot paths.** A product list shows `review_count` and `avg_rating`. Computing them with `count(*)` over millions of reviews on every page view is wasteful, so store them on `product` and update them when a review is written (in the same transaction, by trigger, or asynchronously if staleness is acceptable).
- **Immutable snapshots, which are not really denormalization.** `order_line.unit_price` copies the product's price *at the time of purchase*. It is a different fact from the product's current price, and it must not change when the catalog changes. The same goes for a shipping address on an order.
- **Analytics.** Warehouses deliberately use wide, denormalized tables, because scans over columnar storage are cheap and joins across billions of rows are not.
- **Caching and search.** Redis entries, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch documents and API response caches are denormalized *projections* of the normalized source of truth.
- **Materialized views** (`CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW ...; REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY ...`) let the database own the denormalized copy. `CONCURRENTLY` requires a unique index on the view.

Rules for safe denormalization:
- There is exactly **one source of truth**, and every copy is derived from it.
- Each copy has a named **sync mechanism** (same transaction, trigger, CDC/outbox event, scheduled rebuild) and a known staleness bound.
- There is a **reconciliation job**, or the copy can be rebuilt from the source, because copies *will* drift.

**Star schema (briefly).** Analytical warehouses organize data as a central **fact table** (one row per event or measurement, such as `fact_sales(date_key, product_key, store_key, quantity, revenue)`) surrounded by **dimension tables** (`dim_date`, `dim_product`, `dim_store`) holding descriptive attributes. Dimensions are intentionally denormalized: `dim_product` repeats category and brand names, so queries join each dimension once and filter and group freely. Normalizing the dimensions into sub-tables gives a *snowflake schema*. Slowly changing dimensions, columnar storage and ETL vs ELT are covered in the **OLTP vs OLAP & Warehousing** chapter. The key point here: OLTP schemas are normalized for correct writes, OLAP schemas are denormalized for fast scans, and a pipeline connects them.

sections.title: Soft Deletes: Useful, but Not Free
sections.content:
A **soft delete** marks a row as deleted (`deleted_at timestamptz`, NULL meaning live) instead of removing it. Teams use it for undo/restore, audit trails, and protection against accidental deletes.

The costs are real and often discovered late:
- **Every query must filter it.** Forget `WHERE deleted_at IS NULL` in one place and deleted data reappears in a report, a search result or an API response. Mitigate with views (`live_account`), ORM default scopes, or row-level security policies, and make the filtered path the default.
- **Unique constraints break.** A plain `UNIQUE (email)` prevents a deleted user from signing up again. Use a **partial unique index**: `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ... ON account (email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL`.
- **Foreign keys don't understand it.** A live order can reference a soft-deleted customer, and `ON DELETE CASCADE` never fires. Cascading a soft delete becomes application logic.
- **Bloat.** Tables and indexes keep growing with dead-but-present rows. Partial indexes (`WHERE deleted_at IS NULL`) keep the hot indexes small.
- **Privacy law.** GDPR's right to erasure (and similar laws) generally requires actually deleting or irreversibly anonymizing personal data. A soft delete alone doesn't satisfy that, so you still need a hard-delete or anonymization job with a retention period.

Alternatives that keep the main table clean:
- an **archive table**: move the row on delete (`WITH d AS (DELETE ... RETURNING *) INSERT INTO account_archive SELECT * FROM d`),
- an **audit/history table** populated by trigger, or a temporal (system-versioned) table,
- an **event log** if you are already event-sourcing.

Use soft deletes when users genuinely need restore. Otherwise prefer a hard delete plus an archive.

sections.title: JSONB Columns vs Tables
sections.content:
PostgreSQL's `jsonb` stores JSON in a decomposed binary form that can be indexed and queried (`->`, `->>`, `@>`, jsonpath). It is tempting to put everything in one `data jsonb` column and skip modeling. That trades away most of what the database does for you.

**Good uses of JSONB:**
- **Sparse or variable attributes**: product specs that differ per category (a T-shirt has size and material, a laptop has RAM and ports), user preferences, feature flags.
- **Data you store and return whole but rarely query inside**: webhook payloads, third-party API responses, audit snapshots.
- **Schema that is genuinely owned by someone else**: integration metadata, customer-defined custom fields.

**Keep it in columns and tables when:**
- you **filter, join, sort or aggregate** on it regularly,
- it needs **constraints**: NOT NULL, foreign keys, CHECK, uniqueness. You cannot put a foreign key on a JSON field,
- it has a **type** that matters (money, timestamps). `->>` returns text, so every numeric comparison needs a cast, and the cast errors if one row stores `"lots"`,
- it is **updated independently and frequently**. Updating one key rewrites the entire jsonb value (and its TOASTed storage for large documents), and concurrent writers to different keys of the same row still conflict on the row.

The planner also lacks per-key statistics for JSONB, so row estimates for `attributes->>'color' = 'black'` are guesses. An expression index (`CREATE INDEX ON product ((attributes->>'color'))`) gives it statistics as well as speed.

**The hybrid pattern** is what most mature schemas end up with: core, queried, constrained fields as real columns, plus one `attributes jsonb` for the long tail, indexed with **GIN**. `jsonb_path_ops` is smaller and faster for `@>` containment and jsonpath queries, while the default `jsonb_ops` also supports key-existence operators (`?`, `?|`, `?&`). When a JSON key becomes important (it starts appearing in WHERE clauses everywhere), promote it to a column with an expand/contract migration.

sections.label: Soft delete & JSONB
sections.explanation: The partial unique index is what lets `ana@example.com` sign up again after her first account was soft-deleted, and the view gives queries a default live-rows path. In `product`, price stays a typed, constrained column, while category-specific specs go in `attributes`. `@>` containment can use the GIN index. The `->>` extraction returns text, hence the `::int` cast. All outputs were produced by running the script on PostgreSQL.

sections.title: Schema Migrations Without Downtime: Expand and Contract
sections.content:
In a system with multiple app instances and rolling deploys, old and new code run **at the same time** against the same database. A migration that renames a column breaks every old instance the moment it commits. The fix is **expand/contract** (also called parallel change). Split every breaking change into backward-compatible steps, each deployable and reversible on its own.

Example: rename `student.student_name` to `full_name`.
1. **Expand**: `ALTER TABLE student ADD COLUMN full_name text;` (nullable, no default, instant). Old code ignores it.
2. **Dual-write**: deploy code that writes both columns and still reads the old one.
3. **Backfill** in small batches (`UPDATE ... WHERE id BETWEEN $1 AND $2`, commit each batch) so you never hold locks or generate a huge transaction.
4. **Switch reads** to `full_name`. Verify with metrics or a consistency check, then enforce `NOT NULL`.
5. **Stop writing** the old column. Deploy.
6. **Contract**: `ALTER TABLE student DROP COLUMN student_name;` once no deployed code references it.

PostgreSQL specifics that decide whether a migration is instant or an outage:
- `ADD COLUMN ... DEFAULT <constant>` is metadata-only since PostgreSQL 11. A *volatile* default (`DEFAULT random()`, or `clock_timestamp()`) still rewrites the table.
- `SET NOT NULL` normally scans the whole table under an exclusive lock. Instead, add `CHECK (full_name IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID`, then `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` (which only takes a SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE lock, so reads and writes continue), then `SET NOT NULL`. PostgreSQL 12+ uses the validated CHECK to skip the scan.
- Foreign keys follow the same pattern: `ADD CONSTRAINT ... FOREIGN KEY ... NOT VALID`, then `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT`.
- Build indexes with `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` (it cannot run inside a transaction block, and it leaves an INVALID index to drop if it fails).
- Set `lock_timeout` (e.g. `SET lock_timeout = '5s'`) before DDL. An `ALTER TABLE` waiting for its ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock behind one long query blocks *every* later query on that table, so it is better to fail fast and retry.
- Changing a column's type usually rewrites the table. Use expand/contract with a new column instead.

Tooling: Flyway, Liquibase, Alembic, Prisma Migrate, Rails/Django migrations or Atlas to version migrations; pgroll and Reshape automate expand/contract for PostgreSQL; gh-ost and pt-online-schema-change do online table rebuilds for MySQL. Whatever the tool, review every migration for its **lock level and rewrite behaviour**, not just its SQL.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["1. Expand: add new column, nullable, unused"] --> B["2. Deploy dual-write: write old and new, read old"]
  B --> C["3. Backfill old rows in small batches"]
  C --> D["4. Switch reads to new column, add NOT NULL via NOT VALID then VALIDATE"]
  D --> E["5. Deploy code that stops writing the old column"]
  E --> F["6. Contract: drop old column"]
  A -.->|"safe to roll back"| R["Every step before 6 is reversible"]
  D -.-> R
sections.caption: Expand/contract migration. Old and new application versions can run side by side at every step, which is what makes zero-downtime rolling deploys possible.

sections.title: Document Databases: Embed vs Reference
sections.content:
Document stores (MongoDB, Couchbase, Firestore, DynamoDB's item model) invert the default. Relational modeling starts from the *data* and normalizes. Document modeling starts from the **access patterns** and shapes each document to answer a query in one read. The central decision for each relationship is **embed** (nest the child inside the parent document) or **reference** (store the child separately and keep its id).

| Embed when... | Reference when... |
|---|---|
| The data is read together (an order and its line items) | The child is read or updated on its own |
| The child is owned by the parent and has no identity elsewhere | The child is shared by many parents (an author on many posts) |
| The relationship is one-to-few and **bounded** | The relationship is one-to-many and **unbounded** (comments, events, followers) |
| You want atomic single-document updates | The child changes often and would rewrite a big parent |

Hard limits and failure modes:
- MongoDB documents are capped at **16 MB**, and large documents are slow to read and rewrite long before that. An ever-growing embedded array (all comments on a viral post) is the classic mistake.
- Embedding a **shared** entity duplicates it, which brings back exactly the update anomaly normalization removes. If an author's name is embedded in 10,000 posts, a rename touches 10,000 documents.
- **Extended reference** is the middle ground: store the referenced id plus the few fields you display (`author: {_id, name}`), and accept that those copies need syncing.

Our enrollment example in document form might embed phones in the student document (owned, bounded, read together), and reference courses by `course_code` from an `enrollments` collection (many-to-many, shared, queried from both directions).

Modern document databases support multi-document ACID transactions (MongoDB since 4.0 on replica sets and 4.2 on sharded clusters), but they are slower and the data model is designed to need them rarely. **DynamoDB single-table design** goes further: you list every access pattern up front and design partition and sort keys (and secondary indexes) so that each pattern is a single key lookup or range query. It is very fast at scale, but rigid when a new access pattern appears.

The underlying trade-off is the same one this chapter has been about. Embedding is denormalization: faster reads of the designed path, at the cost of keeping copies consistent.

sections.title: Common Mistakes and Misconceptions
sections.content:
- **Deriving FDs from sample data.** Three rows where every course has one instructor do not prove `course → instructor`. Ask for the business rule, and ask about the future ("could a course ever have two sections?").
- **Surrogate key without a natural UNIQUE.** `id` is unique, but nothing stops two rows for the same email or ISBN. Keep candidate keys unique.
- **Comma-separated lists in a column** (`tags = 'a,b,c'`). You lose indexing, foreign keys and correct counts. Use a child table, or a native array/JSONB with a GIN index if you truly never need constraints.
- **The EAV trap.** `entity_attribute_value(entity_id, attribute, value text)` looks flexible, but it loses types, constraints and sane queries. JSONB or real columns are almost always better.
- **Missing indexes on foreign keys.** PostgreSQL indexes the referenced primary key, not the referencing column. Parent deletes and joins then scan the child table.
- **Polymorphic foreign keys** (`commentable_type, commentable_id`), which no database can enforce. Prefer separate nullable FKs with a CHECK that exactly one is set, or a separate junction table per parent type.
- **Denormalizing before measuring**, or without naming the sync mechanism and owner.
- **"NoSQL means no modeling."** Document modeling is *more* sensitive to design, because the schema encodes your access patterns.
- **Breaking migrations** (rename or retype in one step) during rolling deploys. Expand, migrate, then contract.
- **Over-normalizing values that are snapshots.** An order's price and shipping address must *not* follow later changes to the product or the user profile.

sections.title: Normal forms in one breath
sections.content: **1NF**: one value per cell, no repeating groups, a key. **2NF**: no non-key column depends on just *part* of a composite key. **3NF**: no non-key column depends on another non-key column. **BCNF**: the left side of every functional dependency is a superkey. Memory aid for 3NF: *every non-key attribute depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.* If an interviewer asks "is this table normalized?", list the functional dependencies first, then check each determinant against the keys.

items: **Model first, then normalize:** identify entities, relationships, cardinality and optionality, and turn every business rule into a key, foreign key, UNIQUE or CHECK constraint.

**Many-to-many** relationships become a **junction table** with a foreign key to each side and a key on the pair. It often carries its own attributes (grade, quantity, role) and deserves a business name.

**Keys:** a candidate key is a minimal unique column set. Pick one as primary and enforce the rest with UNIQUE NOT NULL. Prefer a surrogate key (bigint identity or UUIDv7) plus a UNIQUE natural key. Index foreign key columns yourself.
**Functional dependencies** (X → Y) come from business rules. X is a superkey when its closure X⁺ contains every attribute. A table can have several overlapping candidate keys.
**Anomalies** (update, insert, delete) all come from storing a fact in a table whose key does not determine it. Normalization moves each fact next to its determinant.

**1NF** atomic values, **2NF** no partial-key dependencies, **3NF** no transitive dependencies on non-key columns, **BCNF** every determinant is a superkey. 3NF is always reachable while preserving every dependency. BCNF is always lossless, but may lose dependencies.

**Denormalize deliberately:** measure first, keep one source of truth, name the sync mechanism and staleness bound, and be able to rebuild copies. Price and address snapshots on orders are separate facts, not denormalization.

**Soft deletes** need a filter on every query (views or RLS), partial unique indexes, manual cascade logic and a real erasure path for privacy laws. **JSONB** suits sparse or external data. Anything you filter, join or constrain belongs in columns.
**Zero-downtime migrations** use expand → dual-write → backfill → switch reads → contract. In PostgreSQL use NOT VALID + VALIDATE, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, constant defaults and a lock_timeout.
**Document databases** model around access patterns: embed owned, bounded data read together, and reference shared or unbounded data. Embedding is denormalization, with the same consistency costs.

quiz.question: In a table `enrollment(student_id, course_code, student_name, grade)` with key (student_id, course_code), which normal form does `student_id → student_name` violate?
options: 1NF
2NF
3NF only
None, because student_name is atomic
quiz.explanation: student_name is a non-prime attribute that depends on only part of the composite key, which is a partial dependency and the defining 2NF violation. The fix is to move it to student(student_id, student_name).

quiz.question: `course(course_code, course_title, dept_code, dept_name)` has key course_code. Renaming a department requires updating many rows. What is the problem, and what is the fix?
options: A 1NF violation. Split dept_name into first and last parts
A partial dependency. Add dept_code to the primary key
A missing index. Add an index on dept_name
A transitive dependency course_code → dept_code → dept_name (3NF). Move it to department(dept_code, dept_name)
quiz.explanation: dept_name depends on dept_code, a non-key column, so it is a transitive dependency. Storing it on every course causes the update anomaly. Extracting a department table makes the rename a one-row update.

quiz.question: A table is in 3NF but not BCNF. Which situation makes this possible?
options: A non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute
The table has overlapping composite candidate keys, and some FD has a non-superkey determinant whose right side is a prime attribute
The table stores a comma-separated list in one column
The table has a single-column primary key
quiz.explanation: 3NF allows X → A when A is prime (part of some candidate key). BCNF does not. That gap only matters with multiple overlapping candidate keys, such as {student, course} and {student, instructor} with instructor → course.

quiz.question: Why might a designer stop at 3NF rather than decompose a table to BCNF?
options: The BCNF decomposition may not preserve a dependency, so a rule can no longer be enforced by a single table's key
BCNF decompositions are always lossy and lose rows
BCNF forbids foreign keys
BCNF requires every table to have a surrogate key
quiz.explanation: Every relation can be decomposed into BCNF losslessly, but not always in a dependency-preserving way. For example, {student, course} → instructor ends up spanning two tables. 3NF synthesis always preserves dependencies, so some teams keep 3NF, or add a composite foreign key to enforce the lost rule.

quiz.question: You use a surrogate `id bigint` primary key on `users`. What else should you almost always add?
options: A second surrogate key for redundancy
Nothing, because the surrogate key already guarantees uniqueness
A UNIQUE NOT NULL constraint on the natural candidate key, such as email
A trigger that copies id into email
quiz.explanation: The surrogate key only makes the *row id* unique. Without a UNIQUE constraint on the natural key, the same real-world user can be inserted twice under different ids. Keep every candidate key enforced.

quiz.question: How should a many-to-many relationship between students and courses be represented in a relational schema?
options: A text column on student listing course codes separated by commas
A foreign key from course to student
Duplicate the course columns onto the student table
A junction table with foreign keys to both student and course, keyed on the pair (plus attributes like grade)
quiz.explanation: Relational cells hold single values, so M:N needs an associative (junction) table. It enforces both foreign keys, prevents duplicate pairs through its key, and is the natural home for relationship attributes such as grade or enrolled_at.

quiz.question: An `account` table uses soft deletes (`deleted_at`). Users who deleted their account cannot sign up again with the same email. What is the right fix?
options: Drop the uniqueness requirement on email
Replace UNIQUE(email) with a partial unique index `ON account (email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL`
Append a random suffix to the email on signup
Hard-delete all rows nightly
quiz.explanation: A partial unique index enforces uniqueness only among live rows, so a soft-deleted row no longer blocks a new one. Dropping uniqueness allows duplicate live accounts, and mangling emails breaks login and lookups.

quiz.question: Which data is the best fit for a JSONB column rather than separate relational columns?
options: Category-specific product specs (RAM for laptops, size for shirts) that are mostly displayed and occasionally filtered by containment
An order's customer_id, which must reference customers
An account balance that is updated on every transaction
The created_at timestamp used to sort every list view
quiz.explanation: JSONB fits sparse, variable attributes, and a GIN index supports containment queries on them. Foreign keys can't target JSON fields, frequent updates rewrite the whole value, and core sort or filter columns need types, constraints and statistics.

quiz.question: During a rolling deploy you need to rename a column. Which approach avoids breaking running instances?
options: `ALTER TABLE ... RENAME COLUMN` in the same deploy as the code change
Rename the column at night when traffic is low
Add the new column, dual-write, backfill in batches, switch reads, stop writing the old column, then drop it
Create a new table and swap the table names in one transaction
quiz.explanation: Old and new code run at the same time during a rolling deploy. Expand/contract keeps each step backward compatible: old code keeps working until no instance references the old column, and only then is it dropped.

quiz.question: In a document database, when should a blog post's comments NOT be embedded in the post document?
options: When comments are always displayed with the post
When each post has at most three comments
When comments need to be shown in insertion order
When the number of comments is unbounded and comments are queried or moderated on their own
quiz.explanation: Unbounded arrays grow toward the document size limit (16 MB in MongoDB) and make every post rewrite expensive. Comments that are queried independently (moderation queues, a user's comment history) also argue for a separate collection that references the post id.
